Why this matters

Conservation needs more than leaving forests alone.

We believe restrictions on access to roadless areas can make it harder for forestry professionals to assess conditions and respond to problems such as invasive species, dead trees, pests, and wildfire risk.

Forest ecosystems are connected to wildlife habitat, clean water, carbon storage, and the natural cycles that sustain life. The goal should be to protect these resources through informed, responsible stewardship.

“We never truly know what is going on in our forests if we do not investigate and act accordingly.”

What is at stake

Healthy forests support healthy ecosystems.

We believe forests need timely monitoring and appropriate management to help prevent avoidable problems.

01 / FOREST HEALTH

Invasive species

Invasive plants and pests can put pressure on native ecosystems. Monitoring helps identify problems and guide a response.

02 / WILDFIRE RISK

Dead trees and excess brush

We support evaluating forest conditions and considering prescribed fire or other treatments when qualified professionals determine they are appropriate.

03 / WILDLIFE

Habitat and food sources

Forest conditions affect the plants and animals that depend on healthy habitat and functioning food webs.

04 / OUR ENVIRONMENT

Natural cycles

Trees play important roles in oxygen production, carbon storage, and the water and nitrogen cycles.

What we believe

Access for assessment.
Management with purpose.

We believe the 2001 Roadless Conservation Act should be replaced with a policy that ensures forests are regularly assessed and that qualified forestry professionals can recommend appropriate treatments.

01

Annual forest visits

Require foresters to visit and assess forest conditions annually, including areas that are currently difficult to access.

02

Targeted removal

Identify and address invasive species and dead or hazardous trees based on site conditions and professional judgment.

03

Prescribed fire when appropriate

Use small, controlled burns only when planned and carried out by qualified professionals under suitable conditions.

Forest conservation should include active, informed stewardship.

Your voice matters

Three ways to take action.

Community members can ask questions, share concerns, and encourage decision-makers to consider responsible forest management.

✉

Contact your senator

Ask your U.S. senator to consider our proposal to repeal the 2001 Roadless Rule and support a replacement focused on regular forest assessment and management.

Find your senator's contact information ↗
♧

Contact your county forest service agent

Ask how forests in your county are monitored and managed, and what residents can do to support local forest health.

Find an NC Forest Service contact ↗
⌂

Reach out to the USDA

Share your concerns about roadless-area management and encourage the agency to consider practical conservation and forest-health strategies.

Find USDA contact information ↗

Not sure what to say? Start here.

Hello, I am a concerned community member contacting you about forest management and the 2001 Roadless Rule. I encourage you to support regular assessments of forest conditions and responsible management by qualified forestry professionals. Please consider how invasive species, dead trees, and wildfire risk can be addressed while protecting wildlife and ecosystem health. I would appreciate learning your position and what steps your office is taking on this issue. Thank you for your time.
